hierarchyPage.title: The org chart of India
hierarchyPage.subtitle: One simple chart of who answers to whom - from you, the voter, down to your local office. Tap any level to explore the real people in it.
hierarchyPage.youDesc: In a democracy the chart starts with you. Every elected person below works for you, and every appointed officer works under someone you elected.
hierarchyPage.parliamentDesc: Makes national laws. You directly elect your Lok Sabha MP; state legislators choose Rajya Sabha MPs.
hierarchyPage.electsPresident: MPs + state MLAs elect the Head of State
hierarchyPage.presidentAppoints: Appoints the PM who commands the Lok Sabha's confidence
hierarchyPage.pmDesc: Run the country day to day - defence, railways, highways, taxes, telecom. Each minister heads a national department.
hierarchyPage.stateDesc: You elect your MLA; the majority picks the Chief Minister. States run police, schools, hospitals, state roads and water.
hierarchyPage.districtDesc: The Collector / District Magistrate (DM) and the Superintendent of Police (SP) - appointed officers who deliver services and safety in each district.
hierarchyPage.localDesc: Your councillor, sarpanch and ward officers - garbage, drains, local roads, street lights and certificates.
hierarchyPage.judiciaryDesc: Courts (Supreme Court → High Courts → district courts) are independent of everyone above. They answer to the Constitution, not to ministers - that is what keeps the chart honest.
howToItems: Local problem (garbage, drains, streetlight)? Start at the bottom - your local body or ward office.
State subject (police, government school or hospital, state road)? Your MLA and the state government.
National subject (railways, highways, income tax, passports)? Your MP and the Union ministry.
Not solved? Move ONE level up the chart - that is exactly what escalation means.

collector_dm.label: District Collector / DM
collector_dm.handles: Revenue, land, certificates, disaster relief and overall district coordination - the safe catch-all for your area.
collector_dm.escalate: The top district authority. Escalate here when a department does not respond.

sp_district.label: Superintendent of Police (SP)
sp_district.handles: All policing, safety and FIRs in the district.
sp_district.escalate: Police station (the SHO, the officer in charge) → DSP / Circle Officer → Superintendent of Police (SP) → state police chief (DGP). If the station won't file your FIR, a magistrate (judge) can order it - the power is in BNSS Section 175(3).

mun_commissioner.label: Municipal Commissioner
mun_commissioner.handles: All city civic services - roads, water, garbage, drains, lights, property tax.
mun_commissioner.escalate: Ward Officer → Deputy/Zonal Commissioner → Commissioner / grievance cell.

ward_officer.label: Ward Officer / Ward Engineer
ward_officer.handles: Your first stop in a city for potholes, garbage, drains and street lights.
ward_officer.escalate: Start here, then escalate to the Municipal Commissioner.

cdo_ceozp.label: Rural development head (CEO, Zila Parishad / CDO)
cdo_ceozp.handles: Rural development works and government-scheme delivery.
cdo_ceozp.escalate: Block Development Officer (BDO) → CEO of the Zila Parishad (the district rural-development council) → District Collector.

cmo_health.label: Chief Medical Officer (CMO)
cmo_health.handles: Government hospitals, local health centres (PHCs), vaccinations and ambulances.
cmo_health.escalate: Local health-centre doctor (PHC Medical Officer) → Block Medical Officer → Chief Medical Officer (CMO) → Director, Health Services.

deo_education.label: District Education Officer
deo_education.handles: Government schools, teachers, the Right to Education (RTE) and mid-day meals.
deo_education.escalate: Head Teacher → Block Education Officer → DEO → Director, School Education.

ee_pwd.label: Executive Engineer, Public Works Dept (PWD)
ee_pwd.handles: State and district roads and public buildings.
ee_pwd.escalate: Junior Engineer → Assistant Engineer → Executive Engineer → Chief Engineer.

ee_phed.label: Executive Engineer, Water (PHED)
ee_phed.handles: Rural piped water supply (Jal Jeevan Mission).
ee_phed.escalate: Junior Engineer → Assistant Engineer → Executive Engineer → Chief Engineer.

dso_pds.label: District Supply Officer
dso_pds.escalate: Fair Price Shop → Supply Inspector → District Supply Officer → Collector.

bdo.label: Block Development Officer (BDO)
bdo.handles: Rural works, the rural job-guarantee scheme (MGNREGA) and rural housing, at the block level.
bdo.escalate: Gram Panchayat → BDO → CEO Zila Parishad → Collector.

tehsildar_sdm.label: Tehsildar / SDM (Sub-Divisional Magistrate)
tehsildar_sdm.handles: Land records, updating who owns a property after a sale or inheritance (mutation), and certificates - at the tehsil / sub-division office.
tehsildar_sdm.escalate: Village land-record officer (Patwari) → Tehsildar → SDM → Collector.

panchayat_secretary.label: Gram Panchayat Secretary
panchayat_secretary.handles: Village-level civic works, alongside the elected Sarpanch.

discom.label: Electricity Board (DISCOM)
discom.escalate: Use the DISCOM helpline or app: Junior Engineer (JE) → Assistant / Executive Engineer of your division.

nhai.label: NHAI / National Highways
nhai.escalate: Raise via the national grievance portal (CPGRAMS).

chief_secretary.label: Chief Secretary
chief_secretary.handles: The state's top bureaucrat - final administrative escalation.
chief_secretary.escalate: Use after the district and department have failed to respond.

dgp.label: Director General of Police (DGP)
dgp.handles: Head of the state police - final police escalation.
dgp.escalate: Use after the SP has not acted.

cabinet_secretary.label: Cabinet Secretary
cabinet_secretary.handles: The Union government's top bureaucrat (coordinates ministries). Not a citizen contact point.

flag.title: The National Flag of India
flag.intro: India's Tricolour is a precise civic symbol: three equal bands and the Ashoka Chakra at its centre. Explore what each part represents and how the flag came to be adopted.
flag.interactionHint: Hover or tap a detail to see it on the flag.
flag.flagAria: The National Flag of India: saffron, white and green horizontal bands with a navy-blue 24-spoke Ashoka Chakra

structure.title: Its structure
structure.body: A rectangular 2:3 flag, divided into three equal horizontal bands. Saffron is always at the top.

saffron.title: Saffron
saffron.body: The top band represents the strength and courage of the country.

white.title: White
white.body: The middle band stands for peace and truth, with the Dharma Chakra at its centre.

green.title: Green
green.body: The lower band represents the fertility, growth and auspiciousness of the land.

chakra.title: Ashoka Chakra
chakra.body: The navy-blue Dharma Chakra has 24 spokes. Based on the Sarnath Lion Capital, it represents the wheel of law and movement.

adopted.body: The Constituent Assembly adopted the flag in its present form.

independence.body: It became the national flag of the Dominion of India at Independence.

republic.body: It continued as the national flag when India became a Republic.

code.body: The Flag Code was revised, setting out how citizens may display it with dignity.

flag.respectBody: The saffron band is displayed at the top, and the official Flag Code should always be followed.

rights.metaTitle: What are my rights? The Constitution of India in plain language
rights.metaDescription: Every right the Constitution of India gives you, explained simply - the six fundamental rights, your duties, how to enforce a right in court, and how the whole Constitution is built. With the exact article numbers.
rights.title: What are my rights?
rights.subtitle: Every person in India has rights that no government can take away. Here is what the Constitution of India actually gives you - explained simply, with the exact articles so you can always check the source.
rights.disclaimer: This is plain-language civic education, not legal advice. Each right is written into the Constitution of India; the article numbers let you check the original text.

article32.eyebrow: The heart and soul of the Constitution
article32.title: Article 32: your direct line to the highest court
article32.intro: Every right on this page is only as strong as your power to enforce it. Article 32 is that power. If the government breaks one of your Fundamental Rights, Article 32 lets you go straight to the Supreme Court of India to set it right. The right to do this is itself a Fundamental Right, so it can never be taken away.
article32.quote: If I was asked to name any particular article in this Constitution as the most important - an article without which this Constitution would be a nullity - I could not refer to any other article except this one. It is the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it.
article32.quoteBy: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, Constituent Assembly of India, 9 December 1948
what: The right to go straight to the Supreme Court when the State breaks a Fundamental Right. You do not have to start in a lower court first.
The court can issue an order called a writ to force the government to act, or to stop it acting wrongly (the five writs are explained further down this page).
This right cannot be refused. It can only be paused during a formal national Emergency.
when: When a Fundamental Right is broken - for example an unlawful arrest, censorship of your speech, or unfair treatment by a government body.
Against the State or a public authority, not for a private quarrel between two people. Private matters go to the ordinary courts.
You can also go to your State High Court under Article 226. A High Court is usually nearer, and it can protect even more than Fundamental Rights alone.
article32.howTitle: How to use it, step by step
how: Be clear which Fundamental Right was broken, and which government body broke it.
File a writ petition in the Supreme Court under Article 32, or in a High Court under Article 226. A lawyer can help you write it.
If you cannot afford a lawyer, free legal aid is your right (Article 39A). Ask the nearest Legal Services Authority - it costs nothing.
Anyone can file a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) for people who cannot reach the court themselves. Courts have even accepted a simple letter as a petition.
article32.note: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right, which is why it guards all the others. This is plain-language awareness, not legal advice. For a real case, speak to a lawyer or your free Legal Services Authority.
article32.submitTitle: How to submit it to the Supreme Court
article32.submitIntro: A petition under Article 32 is filed in one of two official ways. No email, by itself, counts as filing.
article32.submitEfileText: Use the Supreme Court's official e-filing portal:
article32.submitLetterText: Post it by registered post, with your facts and documents, to the Chief Justice of India at:
article32.submitEmailText: For questions and correspondence only - this does not file a petition:
article32.submitNote: Most people file through a lawyer, and free legal aid (Article 39A) can do it for you at no cost - ask your nearest Legal Services Authority. Always check the official Supreme Court website before you file.

ambedkar.title: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar
ambedkar.intro: India's Constitution was shaped above all by one person - Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar, known to millions as Babasaheb. As Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly, he led the writing of the Constitution of India and is honoured as its chief architect.

facts.label: His role
facts.value: Chairman of the Drafting Committee - the chief architect of the Constitution of India.

facts.label: In government
facts.value: Independent India's first Minister of Law and Justice.

facts.label: The scholar
facts.value: A jurist and economist who earned degrees at Columbia University and the London School of Economics.

facts.label: The reformer
facts.value: A lifelong campaigner against untouchability and caste, and a champion of equal rights for every citizen.

facts.label: Honoured
facts.value: Awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, in 1990.

ambedkar.quote: However good a Constitution may be, it is sure to turn out bad because those who are called to work it happen to be a bad lot. However bad a Constitution may be, it may turn out to be good if those who are called to work it happen to be a good lot.
ambedkar.quoteBy: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, Constituent Assembly, 25 November 1949
ambedkar.quoteNote: The Constitution's success rests on the people who run it - which is exactly why holding leaders to account matters.

preamble.title: The promise the Constitution makes
preamble.intro: The Constitution opens with a promise, made in the name of the people of India. It sets out what the country is meant to be, and the four values every law must serve.
preamble.quote: We, the People of India ... give to ourselves this Constitution.
preamble.identity: India is a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic.
preamble.identityNote: "Socialist" and "Secular" were added later, by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

justice.title: Justice
justice.desc: Social, economic and political - for everyone, not just a few.

liberty.title: Liberty
liberty.desc: Of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.

equality.title: Equality
equality.desc: Of status and of opportunity, whoever you are.

fraternity.title: Fraternity
fraternity.desc: Dignity for each person, and unity for the nation.

fundamental.title: Your six fundamental rights
fundamental.intro: These are guaranteed to you by the Constitution itself. If the state breaks them, you can go straight to court - and the court can strike down the law or the order.

equality.title: Right to Equality
equality.summary: The law treats everyone the same.
equality.means: The state cannot favour you or discriminate against you because of your religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Everyone is equal before the law.
examples: Equal protection of the law for every person
No discrimination in public jobs, shops, wells, roads or bathing places
Untouchability is abolished and punishable (Article 17)
The state grants no titles of nobility (Article 18)

freedom.title: Right to Freedom
freedom.summary: The core freedoms of a free citizen.
freedom.means: You can speak, gather peacefully, move and live anywhere in India, and choose your work - within reasonable limits set by law. You also have protections if you are ever arrested.
examples: Freedom of speech and expression
Assemble peacefully, form associations, move and settle anywhere in India
Practise any profession, trade or business
Protection against arbitrary arrest and detention (Article 22)

exploitation.title: Right against Exploitation
exploitation.summary: No one can be forced, bonded or trafficked.
exploitation.means: Human trafficking, begar (forced unpaid labour) and bonded labour are banned. Children under 14 cannot be made to work in factories, mines or other hazardous jobs.
examples: Human trafficking and forced labour are prohibited
Bonded labour is illegal
No child under 14 in a factory, mine or hazardous work

religion.title: Right to Freedom of Religion
religion.means: You are free to follow, practise and share any religion, or none at all. Every religious community can manage its own affairs, and India has no official state religion.
examples: Freely profess, practise and propagate your faith
Religious groups manage their own affairs and institutions
No one is forced to pay taxes for, or attend, any particular religion

cultural.title: Cultural & Educational Rights
cultural.summary: Your language and culture are protected.
cultural.means: Any community can keep its own language, script and culture. Religious and linguistic minorities can set up and run their own schools and colleges.
examples: Protect your language, script and culture
No denial of admission to a state-aided school on grounds of religion, race, caste or language
Minorities can establish and run their own educational institutions

remedies.title: Right to Constitutional Remedies
remedies.summary: The right that protects all the others.
remedies.means: If any fundamental right is violated, you can go directly to the Supreme Court, which can issue orders (writs) to enforce it. Dr B. R. Ambedkar called this the "heart and soul" of the Constitution.
examples: Move the Supreme Court directly under Article 32
Move your High Court under Article 226 (which also covers ordinary legal rights)
The court can order the state to stop acting, or to act

keyArticles.title: Life, liberty and education
keyArticles.intro: Two articles inside your Right to Freedom do the heaviest lifting in everyday life.

life.title: Right to Life and Personal Liberty
life.desc: No person can be deprived of life or personal liberty except by a fair, just and reasonable procedure established by law. Courts have read this widely - it now includes the right to live with dignity, to privacy, to a clean environment, to health, and to a livelihood.

education.title: Right to Education
education.desc: The state must provide free and compulsory education to every child aged 6 to 14. Added by the 86th Amendment in 2002 and backed by the Right to Education Act, 2009.

remedies.title: What to do if a right is broken
remedies.intro: A right you cannot enforce is only a promise. The Constitution gives you a direct route to the courts, which can issue five kinds of orders, called writs.
remedies.writsTitle: The five kinds of court order (writs)
remedies.writsIntro: A writ is simply a direct order from a court. Which one you need depends on the problem. The old Latin names are still used, but here is what each one actually does:

habeas.name: Habeas Corpus
habeas.desc: If a person is being held without a lawful reason, the court can order that they be brought before it and set free.

mandamus.plain: Make an office do its duty
mandamus.name: Mandamus
mandamus.desc: Orders a government office to do the job the law requires - for example, to issue a document you are clearly entitled to.

prohibition.plain: Stop a court that is overstepping
prohibition.name: Prohibition
prohibition.desc: Tells a lower court or tribunal to stop handling a case it has no power to hear, before it decides it.

certiorari.plain: Undo a wrong order already made
certiorari.name: Certiorari
certiorari.desc: Cancels a decision a lower court or authority has already passed without the power to, or without a fair hearing.

quo.plain: Question someone's claim to a post
quo.name: Quo Warranto
quo.desc: Challenges a person holding a public office they are not legally entitled to, and can have them removed.

practical: Free legal aid - your right if you cannot afford a lawyer (Article 39A; the National Legal Services Authority, NALSA, and district legal-services authorities)
Human Rights Commissions - national and in each state
Commissions for Women, SC / ST, Minorities and Child Rights
The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005, to ask the government for answers
The national grievance portal (CPGRAMS) for public-service complaints

duties.title: Your fundamental duties
duties.intro: Rights come with responsibilities. The Constitution lists the duties every citizen is expected to keep - the other side of the same coin.
items: Respect the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem
Cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle
Protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
Defend the country and serve the nation when called upon
Promote harmony beyond religion, language and region, and reject practices that degrade women
Value and preserve our rich heritage and composite culture
Protect the environment - forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife - and be compassionate to living creatures
Develop a scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry
Safeguard public property and reject violence
Strive towards excellence in every sphere of activity
Provide education to your child or ward aged 6 to 14 (added in 2002)

directive.title: Goals the state must strive for
directive.intro: These are goals set for every government. Courts cannot enforce them directly, but they are fundamental to how the country should be run, and laws are shaped by them.
items: A decent livelihood and a fair sharing of resources (Article 39)
Equal pay for equal work, for women and men alike
Free legal aid, so poverty never blocks justice (Article 39A)
The right to work, to education and to help in old age, sickness and want (Articles 41-43)
A living wage and humane conditions of work
Village panchayats as units of self-government (Article 40)
Protection of the environment, forests and wildlife (Article 48A)

structure.title: How the Constitution is built
structure.intro: The Constitution of India is the longest written constitution in the world, and the supreme law of the land - every other law must obey it.
structure.partsIntro: The text is organised into parts. The ones closest to you as a citizen:
parts: Part II - Citizenship: who is an Indian citizen
Part III - Fundamental Rights: the rights on this page
Part IV - Directive Principles: goals for the state
Part IVA - Fundamental Duties: duties of citizens
Parts V-VI - the Union and the State governments
Part IX & IXA - Panchayats and Municipalities: your local government
structure.schedulesIntro: Schedules are the detailed lists attached to the Constitution. A few you may hear about:
schedules: Seventh Schedule - splits powers between the Union and the states (the Union, State and Concurrent lists)
Eighth Schedule - the 22 official languages (this site speaks all of them)
Eleventh & Twelfth Schedules - the powers of panchayats and municipalities
structure.amendDesc: The Constitution can be amended under Article 368, and has been over a hundred times. But the Supreme Court has held that its "basic structure" - such as democracy, secularism and the rule of law - can never be amended away.
structure.propertyNote: Rights can change too: the Right to Property was a fundamental right until 1978, when the 44th Amendment made it an ordinary legal right (Article 300A).

closing.title: Know who to hold to account
closing.desc: Rights are enforced by the people you elect and the officials you can reach. See who is responsible for what, then find the right office near you.
closing.sourceNote: Source: the Constitution of India. This page is for civic awareness and is not legal advice - for any specific situation, consult a lawyer or the official text.

forLeaders.metaTitle: How to be a good leader
forLeaders.metaDescription: A simple guide for anyone who leads, or wants to. Eight lessons on good leadership: seven timeless ones, each from a real, named source - the Bhagavad Gita, Chanakya's Arthashastra, the Thirukkural, Emperor Ashoka and Mahatma Gandhi - and one written for this site by the person who built it.
forLeaders.title: How to be a good leader
forLeaders.subtitle: This page is for you, whether you already lead or you want to one day. Long ago, India's wisest teachers wrote down how a good leader should be. Their words are gathered here in simple form, each from a real, famous source. The last lesson is not from a book - it is from the person who built this site.
forLeaders.address: Leading is not about being big or powerful. It is about doing good for the people who trusted you with their vote. Read these lessons slowly. They were true a thousand years ago, and they are still true today.

principles.heading: People copy their leaders
principles.quote: Whatever a great person does, common people follow. Whatever standard they set, the world pursues.
principles.explain: People watch their leaders and do the same. If you are honest and calm, people learn to be honest and calm. If you cut corners, they learn to cut corners too. So live the way you want your people to live.

principles.heading: Your people's good is your good
principles.quote: In the happiness of his people lies the ruler's happiness; in their welfare, his welfare. He should treat as good not what pleases him, but what pleases his people.
principles.explain: A leader is not happy when only he is happy. A leader is happy when the people are happy. Before every decision, ask one simple thing: does this make ordinary people's lives better? If it only helps you, drop it.

principles.heading: Be fair to everyone
principles.quote: It is not the spear but the just sceptre that gives a ruler victory, and only if it never bends.
principles.explain: A leader wins by being fair, not by being harsh or strong. Treat everyone the same, rich or poor, those who voted for you and those who did not. One unfair act can break the trust you built over many years.

principles.heading: Work for the people, not for reward
principles.quote: You have a right to your work, but never to its rewards. Do not act only for the results, and do not sit idle either.
principles.explain: Do your duty because it is right, not for money, fame or the next post. Do the work fully and honestly, and let the results come on their own.

principles.heading: First control yourself
principles.quote: Control of the senses comes from giving up greed, anger, pride and other weaknesses. Rulers who did not do this were destroyed along with their kingdoms.
principles.explain: Before you can lead others, you must lead yourself. A leader who cannot control his anger, greed or pride will not last. Stay humble and calm, especially when you have power.

principles.heading: Think of the poorest person first
principles.quote: Recall the face of the poorest and weakest person you have seen, and ask if the step you plan will be of any use to him. Will he gain anything by it? Then your doubt will melt away.
principles.explain: When a choice is hard, do not weigh it by the richest or loudest person in the room. Think of the poorest person you know, and ask: will this help that person? If yes, you are on the right path.

principles.heading: Treat every person as your own family
principles.quote: All people are my children. What I want for my own children, their welfare and happiness, I want for all people too.
principles.explain: A leader belongs to everyone, not only to his own group, religion or supporters. Care for people of every faith, language and region as if they were your own family.

principles.heading: Be human first, and hear the criticism before the praise
principles.quote: Embrace humanity and empathy first. Make sure you understand your criticism before you listen to the praise.
principles.explain: Once you hold office, praise finds you on its own and criticism has to be looked for. So look for it. Stay with what people are unhappy about until you truly understand it - who is affected, and what they need - because understanding that is the part of the job nobody can do for you. The praise will still be there afterwards, and it will be worth more.

forLeaders.closingTitle: The chair is for a short time. Your good work stays.
forLeaders.closingBody: One day your term ends and someone else takes the chair. What stays behind is the good you did and the lives you changed. Lead so that, even after you leave, people say: they were good for us.
forLeaders.ownWordsLabel: Written for this site, not a quotation
forLeaders.sourcesNote: The first seven quotes are each from a real, named and published source, and link to it. Where the words come from a holy book, we have kept the meaning true to the well-known translations. The eighth lesson carries no outside link because it is not a quotation from anywhere - it was written for this site by the person who built it, and is marked that way on the card.

whyCare.metaTitle: Why should I care about politics?
whyCare.metaDescription: You didn't choose to follow politics, but it already shapes your money, your street, your school and your safety. Why a few minutes of attention is worth it, what a good representative actually looks like, and how to start.
whyCare.title: Why should I care?
whyCare.subtitle: You didn't choose to follow politics. But politics already follows you - your money, your street, your child's school. Here is why a few minutes of attention is worth it, and what a good representative actually looks like.
whyCare.note: This is about paying attention, not picking a side. No parties, no verdicts - just how it touches you.

everyday.title: Government isn't far away - it is your daily life
everyday.intro: Every one of these is decided by someone you can name, elect and hold to account.

items.title: Your money
items.desc: Income tax, the GST on everything you buy, the price of petrol and a gas cylinder - all set by people in office.

items.title: Your street
items.desc: Roads, potholes, street lights, drains and clean water are somebody's job, and somebody's budget.

items.title: Your family's future
items.desc: Which government school and hospital you get - and whether they actually work - is a political choice.

items.title: Your safety
items.desc: Police, courts and how quickly an FIR gets filed depend on how the system is run and funded.

items.title: Your work
items.desc: Jobs, small-business rules, crop prices and welfare schemes are all decided, not handed down by fate.

items.title: Your voice
items.desc: Whether your area gets heard in the state capital or in Delhi depends on the person you send there.

ignore.title: What happens when nobody is watching
ignore.intro: Not caring is itself a choice - and it has a price. Usually someone else pays it, and often that someone is you.

items.title: The pressure disappears
items.desc: A representative who is never asked has little reason to show up, spend the local fund, or reply. Attention is what keeps them working.

items.title: Problems stay problems
items.desc: The pothole, the missing teacher, the dry tap - unless someone points to the right office and pushes, nothing moves on its own.

items.title: The organised get served first
items.desc: The loudest and best-connected are heard first. Everyone who looked away waits at the back of the queue.

items.title: You pay either way
items.desc: The taxes still leave your pocket and the decisions still get made. Looking away isn't free - it just costs you the say in them.

power.eyebrow: You have more than one vote
power.title: Your vote is the start, not the end
power.intro: Elections are one day in five years. Between them, you still have real levers - and most people never use them.

items.title: Vote - and vote local
items.desc: Your MLA and ward councillor shape your street more than any national vote. The smaller the election, the bigger your share of it.

items.title: Ask, on the record
items.desc: You can file a Right to Information request and make any public office answer in writing. It is your legal right, not a favour.

items.title: Knock on the right door
items.desc: Half the battle is reaching the office that actually owns the problem - not the one that is easiest to find.

items.title: Check the record
items.desc: Attendance, questions asked, funds spent: judge your representative by what they did, not by what they promised.

items.title: Speak up, together
items.desc: One voice is easy to ignore; a whole street or group raising the same issue is not. Sign, gather, show up - numbers move offices.

good.title: What does a good representative look like?
good.intro: Not their party, and not their promises - what they actually do. These are things you can check, whoever they are.

items.title: They show up
items.desc: Attendance in the house is the most basic duty of the job. Present beats absent.

items.title: They ask questions
items.desc: Raising your area's problems and questioning the government is the work itself, not a favour to you.

items.title: They spend the local fund
items.desc: The MP and MLA development funds are meant for your area - used well, not left to lapse.

items.title: They are reachable
items.desc: A real office, a working number, and someone who actually responds when you reach out.

items.title: They serve everyone
items.desc: Not only the people who voted for them, and not only their own community.

items.title: They are honest on paper
items.desc: Assets and any court cases declared truthfully in their sworn affidavit, on the public record.

items.title: They obey the same law
items.desc: The rules that bind you bind the people who make them, too.

good.note: You can check most of this yourself - a representative's attendance and spending sit on the public record. Judge them by what they do, not by what they promise.

start.title: Small habits of an alert citizen
start.intro: You don't need to become an activist. A democracy stays honest when ordinary people pay a little attention, regularly.

items.title: Know who represents you
items.desc: Learn the names of your MP, your MLA and your local councillor. You cannot hold someone to account if you don't know who they are.

items.title: Follow what they actually do
items.desc: Their attendance, the questions they raise and the money they spend are on the public record. Look past the speeches.

items.title: Vote every time - especially locally
items.desc: The smaller the election, the more your single vote weighs. Never skip a local body or panchayat vote.

items.title: Raise problems the right way
items.desc: Take an issue to the office that owns it, in writing, and escalate calmly if it is ignored. Persistence is a citizen's real power.

items.title: Don't stay silent
items.desc: Talk about local issues with family and neighbours. Awareness spreads from person to person, and a community that pays attention is hard to ignore.

closing.title: A democracy is only as awake as its people
closing.desc: Democracy does not run on election day alone. It runs on ordinary people paying attention between elections - asking, checking, and refusing to look away. That work is not for experts or activists. It is yours, and it belongs to everyone.
closing.note: Non-partisan by nature. This is about your part as a citizen - not about any party, any leader or any side.

guides.hubSubtitle: Plain-language, non-partisan how-to guides for using your rights and understanding your government. Free to read, and every claim is sourced.
guides.hubIntro: Knowing who represents you is the first step. Knowing how to actually use the system - to ask for information, to read what a candidate declares, to get a pothole fixed - is the next. These short guides walk through the everyday tools of Indian citizenship, one at a time.

file-an-rti.title: How to file an RTI request
file-an-rti.subtitle: The Right to Information Act, 2005 lets any citizen ask a public authority for information - and get an answer, usually within 30 days. Here is exactly how to use it.
file-an-rti.metaTitle: How to file an RTI request in India - a step-by-step guide
file-an-rti.metaDescription: A plain-language, step-by-step guide to filing a Right to Information (RTI) request in India: who you can ask, the fee, the 30-day deadline, and how to appeal if you are refused.
file-an-rti.hubSummary: Ask any public office for information and get a reply in 30 days. Fees, format, and how to appeal.
file-an-rti.disclaimer: This is general civic information, not legal advice. Fees and formats vary a little by state and authority, so always check the specific public authority's own RTI page.
file-an-rti.intro: The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 gives every Indian citizen the right to ask a government body for information and to receive a reply, usually within 30 days. You do not need a reason, a lawyer, or a special form - a plain application and a small fee are enough.

sections.heading: What you can ask for
body: You can ask any "public authority" - a central or state department, a ministry, a municipal body, a panchayat, a public-sector bank, a government school or hospital, or any body substantially funded by the government - for information it holds.
That includes records, documents, file notings, emails, contracts, reports, and inspection of works or records. You can ask for the reasons behind a decision, not just the decision itself.

There are narrow exemptions (Section 8) - for example information that would harm national security, a live investigation, or personal privacy with no public interest. Even then, if only part of a file is exempt, the rest must still be given to you.

sections.heading: Who to address it to
body: Every public authority has a Public Information Officer (PIO). Your application goes to the PIO of the office that holds the information you want.
If you are not sure which office holds it, send it to the one most likely to - if they do not hold it, the Act requires them to transfer your application to the correct authority within five days.

sections.heading: How to write it
body: There is no prescribed national form. A plain sheet of paper or a simple typed letter is valid, and many states also offer an online portal.
steps: Address it to "The Public Information Officer" of the relevant office.
Write your questions clearly and specifically - one point per question, and ask for documents by name or date range where you can.
State clearly that you are filing under the Right to Information Act, 2005.
Give your name and a postal address for the reply; an email address helps too.
Attach the fee, and keep a copy of the whole application for your records.

sections.heading: The fee
body: For central government bodies the application fee is Rs 10, paid by cash, postal order, demand draft, or online where available. State fees are similar but can differ, so check the authority's own rules.

If you are below the poverty line (BPL), you are exempt from the fee - attach a copy of your BPL card. There may be small per-page charges for photocopies, which the PIO will tell you about before sending large records.

sections.heading: How long it takes
body: The PIO must reply within 30 days of receiving your application.
If the information concerns the life or liberty of a person, the reply must come within 48 hours.
If the PIO does not reply in time, that is treated as a "deemed refusal" - and it gives you the right to appeal.

sections.heading: If you are refused or ignored
body: A refusal, a partial answer, or silence is not the end of the road. The Act builds in a free, two-step appeal.
steps: First appeal: within 30 days, write to the "First Appellate Authority" - a senior officer in the same public authority. There is no fee.
Second appeal: if you are still not satisfied, within 90 days you can appeal to the Central or State Information Commission, an independent body.
The Information Commission can order the information released, and can fine a PIO up to Rs 25,000 for wrongly denying or delaying it.

faq.q: Do I have to say why I want the information?
faq.a: No. The Act specifically says you cannot be asked for your reasons - only for the contact details needed to reply to you.

faq.q: Can I file from anywhere in India?
faq.a: Yes. You can file with any public authority in the country; you do not have to live in that state or district.

faq.q: Can a company or association file an RTI?
faq.a: The right is given to citizens. You can help someone file, but the applicant should be an individual citizen rather than a company or association.

how-a-bill-becomes-law.title: How a bill becomes a law
how-a-bill-becomes-law.subtitle: Every law in India starts as a bill and travels through a fixed set of steps before it can bind anyone. Here is that journey, step by step.
how-a-bill-becomes-law.metaTitle: How a bill becomes a law in India - the legislative process explained
how-a-bill-becomes-law.metaDescription: A clear, plain-language explanation of how a bill becomes law in India: the three readings, both Houses of Parliament, committees, the President's assent, and the different kinds of bills.
how-a-bill-becomes-law.hubSummary: From a draft bill to an Act: the three readings, both Houses, committees, and the President's assent.
how-a-bill-becomes-law.intro: A "bill" is a draft law. Before it can bind citizens it must be passed in the same form by the law-making body - both Houses of Parliament for a central law, or the state legislature for a state law - and then receive assent from the President or Governor.

sections.heading: Where a bill begins
body: Most bills are "Government bills", introduced by a minister. A bill introduced by any other member is a "Private Member's bill"; both follow the same broad path, though very few private member's bills become law.
A bill can start in either House of Parliament - the Lok Sabha (House of the People) or the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) - with one exception: a Money Bill can only start in the Lok Sabha.

sections.heading: The three readings
body: First reading: the bill is introduced and its title and aims are read out. There is usually no debate at this stage.
Second reading: the heart of the process. Members debate the bill's principles and then its clauses one by one, proposing and voting on amendments.
Third reading: the House votes on the bill as a whole. If it passes, it moves to the other House.

sections.heading: The role of committees
body: A bill is often referred to a Parliamentary Committee - a smaller group of MPs who examine it in detail, take expert and public views, and suggest changes.
Committees do much of the careful, less visible work of law-making, and their reports shape the final text before the full House votes.

sections.heading: Both Houses must agree
body: A bill must be passed by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha in the same form.
If the two Houses disagree, the President can summon a rare "joint sitting" of both Houses to resolve the deadlock - though this has happened only a handful of times.
A Money Bill is different: the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes, and the Lok Sabha may accept or reject them.

sections.heading: Assent and commencement
body: Once both Houses pass a bill, it goes to the President, who can give assent (making it an Act), withhold assent, or return a non-Money Bill for reconsideration - but if Parliament passes it again, the President must sign.
An Act usually names the date it comes into force, or lets the government notify that date later. Only then does it actually apply.

sections.heading: State laws work the same way
body: In a state, a bill passes through the Legislative Assembly (and the Legislative Council, where one exists) and then goes to the Governor for assent.
The Governor may also reserve certain bills for the President's consideration.

faq.q: What is the difference between a bill and an Act?
faq.a: A bill is a proposal. It becomes an Act - an enforceable law - only after both Houses pass it and it receives assent.

When Parliament is not in session and immediate action is needed, the President can issue an Ordinance with the force of law. It must be approved by Parliament within six weeks of it reassembling, or it lapses.
A bill dealing only with taxes, government spending, or borrowing. It can start only in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha's role is limited to recommendations.

your-local-body.title: Your local body: what your ward actually controls
your-local-body.subtitle: The pothole, the water supply, the garbage, the birth certificate - most of daily life is run by your local government, not your MP or MLA. Here is who does what.
your-local-body.metaTitle: Local government in India - what your municipality or panchayat controls
your-local-body.metaDescription: Understand India's third tier of government: what a Municipal Corporation, Municipality, or Gram Panchayat actually does, how it differs from an MLA or MP, and how to raise a ward-level complaint.
your-local-body.hubSummary: Water, roads, garbage, certificates: what your municipality or panchayat runs, and how to complain.
your-local-body.intro: India has three tiers of elected government. Below the country's MPs and the state's MLAs sits a third, closest tier - your local body - which the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments made a permanent part of the system. It runs much of what you actually notice day to day.

sections.heading: Two kinds of local body
body: In cities and towns, urban local bodies run things: a Municipal Corporation (big cities), a Municipal Council (smaller towns), or a Nagar Panchayat (areas becoming towns).
In villages, the three-tier Panchayati Raj system does: the Gram Panchayat (village), the Panchayat Samiti (block), and the Zila Parishad (district).

sections.heading: What your ward councillor or panch does
body: You elect a councillor (in a city) or a ward member and Sarpanch (in a village) for your ward - the smallest unit of local government.
They are your first point of contact for local, physical, everyday problems, and they vote on the local body's budget and works.

sections.heading: What the local body actually controls
body: Local water supply, street lighting, local roads and drains, sanitation and garbage collection, public health and local markets, parks, and birth and death certificates.
The Constitution's Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules list the subjects that can be handed to rural and urban bodies - from drinking water and roads to primary schools and slum improvement.

sections.heading: What it does NOT control
body: Big highways, state-wide policing, power generation, and state policy are run by the state government through your MLA and the state departments.

National matters - defence, railways, income tax, foreign policy - belong to the central government, through your MP. Sending a garbage complaint to your MP rarely gets it fixed faster than telling the local body.

sections.heading: How to raise a complaint
body: Because these are local subjects, the fastest route is almost always the local body itself, not a higher representative.
steps: Start with your ward councillor or the local body's ward office - many now have an app, a helpline, or an online complaint portal.
Note down the complaint number they give you; it is your proof and your tracking reference.
If nothing happens, escalate to the ward officer, then the Municipal Commissioner (urban) or the Block Development Officer (rural).
For services with a legal time limit under your state's Public Services Guarantee Act, a missed deadline can itself be escalated.

faq.q: Who do I contact for a broken streetlight or uncollected garbage?
faq.a: Your urban local body (municipality or corporation) or its ward office - not your MLA or MP. These are local-body subjects.

faq.q: Are local body elections really important?
faq.a: Very. This tier decides the services you use most, and turnout is often low - so each vote tends to carry more weight, not less.
The Gram Sabha is the assembly of all adult voters in a village. It approves plans and budgets and can question the Gram Panchayat directly - a rare form of direct democracy.

read-an-election-affidavit.title: How to read an election affidavit
read-an-election-affidavit.subtitle: Every candidate for Parliament or a state assembly files a sworn affidavit declaring their assets, debts, education, and any criminal cases. Here is how to read one - carefully, and fairly.
read-an-election-affidavit.metaTitle: How to read a candidate's election affidavit in India
read-an-election-affidavit.metaDescription: A neutral guide to reading the sworn affidavit (Form 26) every election candidate in India files with the ECI: assets, liabilities, education, and "declared cases" - and what a pending case does and does not mean.
read-an-election-affidavit.hubSummary: Assets, debts, education, pending cases: how to read a candidate's sworn ECI affidavit without jumping to conclusions.
read-an-election-affidavit.disclaimer: This guide explains a public document. A declared court case is an allegation a court is still examining, not a conviction. Reading these figures is about information - never a verdict.
read-an-election-affidavit.intro: Since a 2003 Supreme Court ruling, every candidate for the Lok Sabha or a state assembly must file a sworn affidavit - Form 26 - with the Election Commission when they file their nomination. It is a public document, and it is one of the most useful things a voter can read.

sections.heading: What the affidavit contains
body: Form 26 declares, on oath, the candidate's assets (their own and their spouse's and dependants'), their liabilities (loans and dues), their educational qualifications, and any criminal cases against them.
Because it is sworn, filing false information is itself an offence - which is part of what makes the document worth reading.

sections.heading: Assets and liabilities
body: Assets are split into movable (cash, deposits, jewellery, vehicles, investments) and immovable (land and buildings). Liabilities are what they owe - bank loans, government dues, and so on.

Large assets are not, by themselves, evidence of wrongdoing, and modest assets are not proof of honesty. It is more telling to look at how the figures change between elections, and whether the change is explained.

sections.heading: The "declared cases" section - read this carefully
body: The affidavit lists criminal cases in two parts: cases where a court has already "framed charges" (decided there is enough to put the person on trial), and cases where charges are only alleged.
A declared case means a trial is pending. In Indian law a person is presumed innocent until convicted, so a pending case is not a conviction and must not be read as one.
A separate part lists any past convictions. That is a different thing from a pending case, and the affidavit keeps the two apart for a reason.

sections.heading: Education and other details
body: The affidavit states the candidate's highest qualification and institution. There is no minimum education requirement to contest an election in India, so this is context, not a pass-or-fail test.
It also records age, and the income-tax and PAN details of the candidate and family.

sections.heading: Where to find and check it
body: The signed affidavit is a public record. The Election Commission publishes candidate affidavits, and non-profit groups compile them into searchable form.
Prefer the original scanned affidavit on the ECI record over any second-hand summary, and note which election it was filed for - the figures are a snapshot of that moment.

faq.q: Does a pending case mean the candidate is guilty?
faq.a: No. It means a court is examining an allegation. Under the law the person is innocent unless and until a court convicts them.

faq.q: Is a candidate with more assets a worse choice?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The affidavit is information, not a scorecard. It tells you what was declared; the judgement is yours to make.

faq.q: What if a candidate lies on the affidavit?
faq.a: Filing a false affidavit is a punishable offence, and a rival or a citizen can bring it to the notice of the Election Commission or the courts.

audits.title: CAG audit reports
audits.hubIntro: The Comptroller and Auditor General is the constitutional auditor of India. It examines how governments spend public money and places its reports before Parliament or the State legislature, where the Public Accounts Committee takes them up. Every report below is the CAG’s own, listed with its report number and audit period and linked to the original PDF on the CAG’s website.
audits.metaDescription: Published Comptroller and Auditor General reports for the Union government and every state and Union Territory, linked to the original PDFs on cag.gov.in.
audits.caveat: A CAG report audits a department, not a person. It covers the period stated, which may be before or after the current office-holder took charge. Audit observations are placed before the legislature and examined by the Public Accounts Committee - they are not court findings, and they are not convictions.
audits.scope: Every government is listed - the Union and all {states} states and Union Territories - whichever party governs it.
audits.govTitleUnion: CAG reports on the Union Government
audits.govTitleState: CAG reports on the Government of {state}
audits.govIntroUnion: Reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General on the Union government, as tabled in Parliament.
audits.govIntroState: Reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General on the Government of {state}, as tabled in the State legislature.
audits.emptyGov: No CAG report for this government is indexed here yet. The Comptroller publishes all of its reports on its own site.
audits.personUnion: The Comptroller and Auditor General audits the accounts of the Union government and reports to Parliament, which refers the findings to the Public Accounts Committee.
audits.personState: The Comptroller and Auditor General audits the accounts of the {state} government and reports to the State legislature, which refers the findings to the Public Accounts Committee.

audits.extractNote: These sentences are quoted from the report itself. Each one was located in the PDF before being published here - open the report at the page shown to read it in context.
audits.sourceNote: Report details and links are taken from the Comptroller and Auditor General. Each entry was seeded from a publicly compiled index of CAG reports at {compiler}, then checked against cag.gov.in - entries whose PDF could not be confirmed on the Comptroller’s own site were dropped. Nothing beyond the report number, title, audit period and PDF link is carried over: no severity labels, no scores and no summaries.
